entries.label: Atomic structure: protons, neutrons, electrons, and isotopes

content.value: An atom is built from three particles. Protons and neutrons sit in a tiny, dense nucleus and account for essentially all of the atom's mass; electrons occupy the much larger volume of space around the nucleus and account for essentially none of it. The atomic number, Z, is the number of protons, and it is what identifies the element — every carbon atom in the universe has exactly 6 protons, and any atom with 6 protons is carbon, no matter how many neutrons or electrons it has. The mass number, A, is the total count of protons plus neutrons (nucleons) in a particular nucleus, so A minus Z gives the neutron count. A neutral atom has electrons equal in number to protons; an ion is an atom that has gained or lost electrons, which changes its charge but not its identity, since Z never changes when electrons move. Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same Z) with different numbers of neutrons, and therefore different A — carbon-12, carbon-13, and carbon-14 are all carbon, differing only in mass. Isotope notation writes A as a superscript and Z as a subscript to the left of the element symbol, or simply as the element name followed by the mass number, as in "carbon-14".

entries.label: Types of radioactive decay and how each changes the nucleus

content.value: A nucleus that is unstable — too large, or with the wrong ratio of neutrons to protons — sheds energy and particles until it reaches a stable configuration, and it does this in one of a few characteristic ways. Alpha decay ejects an alpha particle, which is a helium-4 nucleus (2 protons and 2 neutrons bound together). This lowers the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2, so the resulting daughter nuclide is a different element, two places earlier on the periodic table. Beta-minus decay converts a neutron in the nucleus into a proton, an electron, and an antineutrino; the electron (the beta particle) is ejected, so the mass number is unchanged, but the atomic number increases by 1 — the daughter is one element later on the periodic table. Beta-plus (positron) decay does the reverse at the particle level: a proton converts into a neutron, a positron, and a neutrino, so the atomic number decreases by 1 while the mass number again stays the same. Gamma decay is different in kind from the other two: it emits a high-energy photon from a nucleus that is left in an excited (higher-energy) state after an earlier alpha or beta emission, and since a photon carries no protons or neutrons, gamma decay changes neither Z nor A — it only lets the nucleus shed excess energy and settle into its ground state. Alpha particles are the most massive and most ionizing but the least penetrating (stopped by paper or skin); beta particles are lighter, more penetrating (stopped by a few millimeters of metal or plastic); gamma rays carry no mass or charge at all and are the most penetrating, requiring thick lead or concrete for shielding.

entries.label: Half-life and exponential decay

content.value: Radioactive decay is a random process at the level of a single nucleus — there is no way to predict when one particular atom will decay — but across a large sample of identical nuclei, a fixed fraction decays in any given time interval, and that regularity is what makes half-life a useful, precise number. The half-life of an isotope is the time it takes for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay, and it is a fixed property of the isotope: it does not depend on the sample's size, temperature, pressure, or chemical form. The defining trap of this topic is that half-life decay is exponential, not linear: the same fraction (one half) is lost in each successive half-life interval, but because that fraction is applied to a shrinking amount, the absolute quantity lost keeps getting smaller. If a sample starts at 100 grams, the first half-life removes 50 grams (leaving 50), but the second half-life removes only 25 grams (leaving 25), not another 50. The general relationship is N = N₀ × (1/2)^(t / t½), where N₀ is the starting quantity, N is the quantity remaining after elapsed time t, and t½ is the half-life. The exponent t / t½ is simply the number of half-lives that have elapsed, and it does not need to be a whole number — the formula works for a sample that has aged 1.5 or 2.3 half-lives just as well as for one that has aged exactly 3.

entries.label: Balancing nuclear equations

content.value: A nuclear equation is balanced by conserving two separate totals across the arrow: the sum of the mass numbers (the A's) on the left must equal the sum of the mass numbers on the right, and the sum of the atomic numbers (the Z's) on the left must equal the sum of the atomic numbers on the right. This is different from balancing a chemical equation, where individual elements are conserved — here it is nucleon count and charge that are conserved, and the identity of the elements involved is a consequence of that bookkeeping, not an input to it. An alpha particle is written as a helium-4 nucleus, contributing A = 4 and Z = 2; a beta-minus (electron) particle contributes A = 0 and Z = -1; a beta-plus (positron) contributes A = 0 and Z = +1; a gamma photon contributes A = 0 and Z = 0. To balance an equation with an unknown daughter product, add up the known A's and Z's on one side, match the totals on the other side, solve for the unknown nuclide's A and Z, and then use the resulting Z to look up which element that is on the periodic table — the mass number alone never tells you the element, only the atomic number does.

entries.label: Nuclear fission and nuclear fusion

content.value: Fission and fusion both release energy from the nucleus, but they do it by moving nucleons in opposite directions. Fission splits one large, heavy nucleus (typically uranium-235 or plutonium-239) into two smaller nuclei, releasing additional neutrons and a large amount of energy in the process; in a reactor, a neutron striking a fissile nucleus triggers the split, and the neutrons released by that split can go on to trigger further fissions in neighboring nuclei, producing a chain reaction. A reactor sustains this at a controlled, steady rate using a moderator (commonly water) to slow the fast neutrons down to speeds more likely to cause further fission, and control rods made of a strongly neutron-absorbing material (such as boron or cadmium) that are inserted or withdrawn to absorb some of the free neutrons and hold the reaction rate steady rather than letting it run away. Fusion goes the other direction, combining two light nuclei (in stars, mostly hydrogen) into one heavier nucleus, again releasing energy. Fusion is what powers the Sun and other stars: at the enormous temperatures and pressures in a stellar core, hydrogen nuclei are moving fast enough, and packed closely enough, to overcome the strong electrostatic repulsion between their positive charges and get close enough for the strong nuclear force to bind them together. Both processes release energy because they move nuclei toward iron-56, the nucleus with the highest binding energy per nucleon — splitting something heavier than iron or fusing something lighter than iron both release energy, which is why fission works for uranium and fusion works for hydrogen but neither process releases net energy the other way around.

sections.heading: Worked example: how much of a medical radioisotope dose remains?

entries.label: Scenario

content.value: A hospital's radiopharmacy prepares 20.0 mg of technetium-99m, a radioisotope widely used in medical imaging, which has a half-life of 6 hours. Because of a scheduling delay, the prepared dose sits in storage for 30 hours before a technician is ready to use it. How much technetium-99m remains at that point, and what fraction of the original amount is that?

entries.label: Step 1 — identify the given values and the formula

content.value: The starting quantity is N₀ = 20.0 mg. The half-life is t½ = 6 hours. The elapsed time is t = 30 hours. The relationship to use is N = N₀ × (1/2)^(t / t½), where N is the quantity remaining after time t. The exponent t / t½ is the number of half-lives that have elapsed, so the first real task is to convert 30 hours into a number of half-lives rather than plugging hours directly into the formula.

entries.label: Step 2 — find the number of half-lives elapsed

content.value: Number of half-lives = t / t½ = 30 hours / 6 hours per half-life = 5. So 30 hours is exactly 5 half-lives of technetium-99m — a clean whole number in this case, which will make the arithmetic easy to check by repeated halving as well as by the formula.

entries.label: Step 3 — compute the remaining quantity

content.value: Using the formula: N = 20.0 mg × (1/2)^5 = 20.0 mg × (1/32) = 0.625 mg. As a check, halve the sample five times, once per 6-hour interval: 20.0 mg at t = 0 → 10.0 mg at t = 6 h → 5.00 mg at t = 12 h → 2.50 mg at t = 18 h → 1.25 mg at t = 24 h → 0.625 mg at t = 30 h. Both methods agree: 0.625 mg of technetium-99m remains after 30 hours.

entries.label: Conclusion

content.value: The remaining fraction is 0.625 mg / 20.0 mg = 1/32 = 0.03125, or about 3.1% of the original dose — equivalently, about 96.9% of the technetium-99m has decayed by the time the delayed dose is used. This is also why medical imaging isotopes like technetium-99m are deliberately chosen to have short half-lives on the order of hours rather than years: a short half-life means the isotope decays away quickly after the scan, minimizing the patient's total radiation exposure, but it also means a delay of even one day can waste most of a prepared dose, which is exactly the operational problem this scenario illustrates.

entries.label: Treating half-life decay as linear instead of exponential

content.value: The single most common error on this topic is subtracting a fixed percentage per half-life instead of halving what remains. If half of a sample decays in one half-life, it is tempting to reason that the whole sample must be gone after two half-lives (50% + 50% = 100%), but that is linear thinking applied to an exponential process. The correct reasoning re-applies the same 50% reduction to whatever is left: after one half-life, 50% remains; after two, half of that 50% remains, or 25%; after three, half of 25%, or 12.5%; and so on. A sample never mathematically reaches exactly zero through this process — it only approaches zero, halving forever. A fast sanity check for any "remaining amount" problem: after n half-lives, the remaining fraction is (1/2)ⁿ, so 1 half-life leaves 1/2, 2 leaves 1/4, 3 leaves 1/8, 4 leaves 1/16, and 5 leaves 1/32 — never a value found by simple subtraction.

entries.label: Mixing up how alpha, beta, and gamma decay change the nucleus

content.value: Each decay type changes the mass number and atomic number in a specific, memorizable way, and mixing them up is a frequent source of wrong answers. Alpha decay changes both: mass number drops by 4 and atomic number drops by 2, because a whole helium-4 nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons) leaves. A common error is forgetting the atomic-number change and thinking alpha decay only reduces mass while leaving the element the same — but losing 2 protons always means becoming a different element, two places earlier on the periodic table. Beta-minus decay changes only the atomic number, increasing it by 1, while the mass number stays exactly the same, because a neutron converts into a proton (the newly created electron is ejected, not retained in the nucleus) — the error to watch for is assuming any beta emission changes the mass number, when a nucleon is transformed, not lost. Gamma decay changes neither number at all; it is easy to mistakenly credit gamma emission with changing the element, but a photon carries away energy only, never protons or neutrons, so the nuclide's identity is unchanged before and after.

entries.label: Conserving mass number but forgetting atomic number (or the reverse)

content.value: A nuclear equation has two separate conservation checks, and a common mistake is doing only one of them — usually getting the mass numbers to add up correctly while leaving the atomic numbers unbalanced, or vice versa. For example, writing an alpha decay so that the daughter's mass number correctly drops by 4 but its atomic number is left unchanged (rather than dropping by 2) produces an equation that looks balanced at a glance but assigns the daughter nuclide to the wrong element entirely, since it is the atomic number, not the mass number, that determines which element a nuclide is. The reliable habit is to write out and check both totals explicitly every time: add every mass number on the left, add every mass number on the right, and confirm they match; separately add every atomic number on the left and on the right and confirm those match too. Only after both totals check out should the unknown nuclide's atomic number be used to identify the element from the periodic table — never infer the element from the mass number, and never assume an equation is correct just because one of the two totals happens to work out.

entries.label: Confusing fission with fusion, or their real-world conditions

content.value: Fission and fusion are opposite processes — fission splits a heavy nucleus apart, fusion joins light nuclei together — and it is a frequent error to swap which one describes the Sun versus which one describes a nuclear power plant on Earth. Stars, including the Sun, are powered by fusion, not fission: hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium under the star's extreme core temperature and pressure. Commercial nuclear power plants, by contrast, generate electricity through controlled fission of uranium or plutonium — there is currently no commercial fusion power plant supplying electricity to a grid, since sustaining and containing fusion conditions on Earth remains a major unsolved engineering challenge, even though the physics is well understood. A second common error is assuming that combining or splitting any two nuclei always releases energy regardless of which elements are involved; energy release depends on where the nuclei sit relative to iron-56, the most tightly bound nucleus — fusing elements lighter than iron releases energy (as in stars), and splitting elements heavier than iron releases energy (as in a reactor), but fusing very heavy elements or splitting very light ones would require energy input rather than releasing it.

entries.label: Periodic table organization and periodic trends

content.value: The periodic table is organized by atomic number, and its shape encodes electron configuration. A period (row) corresponds to the principal energy level currently being filled, so moving across a period adds electrons to the same outer shell. A group (column) collects elements that end their electron configuration the same way, so elements in a group share a valence-electron count and, with it, similar chemical behavior — group 1 atoms all have one valence electron and form 1+ ions, group 17 atoms all have seven and form 1− ions. Metals occupy the left and center of the table, nonmetals the upper right, and a staircase of metalloids runs along the boundary between them; the noble gases in group 18 have a full outer shell and are chemically inert. Three trends follow from one underlying cause — how strongly the nucleus pulls on the outermost electrons, which is called effective nuclear charge. Atomic radius shrinks moving left to right across a period, because each added proton pulls the same outer shell in tighter, and it grows moving down a group, because each row adds a whole new shell farther from the nucleus. Ionization energy — the energy needed to remove the outermost electron — runs the opposite direction: it rises left to right (electrons held tighter are harder to remove) and falls top to bottom (electrons farther from the nucleus, and shielded by more inner shells, are easier to remove). Electronegativity — an atom's pull on electrons it is sharing in a bond — follows the same left-to-right, bottom-to-top increase as ionization energy, peaking at fluorine in the upper right (noble gases are excluded, since they do not normally form bonds). A useful shortcut: the single most electronegative element sits at the top right of the reactive part of the table, and the least electronegative reactive elements sit at the bottom left, so electronegativity increases diagonally toward fluorine.

entries.label: Ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding

content.value: A chemical bond forms because atoms lower their overall energy by rearranging valence electrons, and the way they rearrange them defines the bond type. Ionic bonding transfers one or more electrons from a metal (low electronegativity, low ionization energy, easily gives up electrons) to a nonmetal (high electronegativity, readily accepts electrons), producing a positive cation and a negative anion that attract each other electrostatically; the result is a rigid lattice, not a discrete pair of atoms, which is why ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct electricity only when the ions are free to move, as in a melt or an aqueous solution. Covalent bonding shares a pair of electrons between two nonmetal atoms rather than transferring them outright; when the two atoms are identical or very close in electronegativity the sharing is even (nonpolar covalent), and when one atom pulls harder on the shared pair the bond is polar covalent, with a partial negative charge on the more electronegative atom and a partial positive charge on the other. Metallic bonding occurs between metal atoms, whose valence electrons delocalize into a shared "sea" surrounding a lattice of positive metal cores; because those electrons are not tied to any one atom, metals conduct electricity and heat well and can be bent or hammered into new shapes (malleable and ductile) without breaking, unlike a brittle ionic crystal. Electronegativity difference between the two bonded atoms is the standard predictive tool: a difference above roughly 1.7 to 2.0 (Pauling scale) is treated as ionic, a difference from about 0.4 up to that cutoff is polar covalent, and a difference below about 0.4 is nonpolar covalent. That number is a heuristic, not a law, so it should always be checked against which kinds of elements are actually bonding — see the common-mistakes section below.

entries.label: Drawing Lewis dot structures

content.value: A Lewis structure shows every valence electron in a molecule or ion as either a bonding pair (drawn as a line between two atoms) or a lone pair (drawn as two dots on one atom), so that every atom (other than hydrogen) ends up surrounded by eight electrons — the octet rule. The procedure has four steps. First, count total valence electrons: add the group number of every atom present, and for a polyatomic ion, add one electron for each unit of negative charge or subtract one for each unit of positive charge. Second, choose a skeleton: the least electronegative nonhydrogen atom is usually placed in the center (it can share electrons in more directions), hydrogen is always terminal (it can hold only one bond), and a single bond — one shared pair — connects the central atom to each surrounding atom. Third, complete octets on the outer atoms first by adding lone pairs, then place any electrons left over on the central atom. Fourth, if the central atom still has fewer than eight electrons around it, convert one or more of an outer atom's lone pairs into a second (or third) shared pair with the central atom, forming a double or triple bond, until the central atom also reaches an octet. Two exceptions to memorize: hydrogen is satisfied with two electrons, not eight, and elements in period 3 or below (such as sulfur or phosphorus) can hold more than eight electrons around them (an expanded octet) because they have accessible d-orbitals — sulfur in sulfur hexafluoride is a standard example, with six bonding pairs and no lone pairs.

entries.label: VSEPR theory and molecular geometry

content.value: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory predicts a molecule's three-dimensional shape from one simple idea: the electron domains around a central atom — each bonding pair (single, double, or triple bond all count as one domain) and each lone pair — repel each other and spread out as far apart as geometry allows. Counting the domains around the central atom gives the electron-domain geometry: two domains arrange linearly (180°), three arrange trigonal planar (120°), four arrange tetrahedral (109.5°), five arrange trigonal bipyramidal, and six arrange octahedral (90°). The molecular geometry — the shape described by the positions of the atoms alone, ignoring lone pairs — matches the electron-domain geometry only when every domain is a bonding pair. When one or more domains are lone pairs, the atoms occupy only some of the positions and the molecular geometry gets a different name even though the electron domains are still spread out the parent way: four domains with one lone pair gives a trigonal pyramidal molecule (ammonia, NH₃), and four domains with two lone pairs gives a bent molecule (water, H₂O), even though both start from a tetrahedral electron-domain arrangement. Lone pairs also occupy more space than bonding pairs, because they are held by only one nucleus instead of being pulled taut between two, so they compress the bond angles between the remaining bonding pairs slightly below the ideal value — water's measured bond angle is about 104.5°, not the full 109.5° of a perfect tetrahedron.

entries.label: The mole concept and molar mass

content.value: The mole is chemistry's counting unit, defined as exactly the number of particles in Avogadro's number, 6.022 × 10²³, and it exists to bridge two size scales: atomic mass units, in which individual atoms and molecules are conveniently weighed, and grams, the scale of a laboratory balance. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, expressed in grams per mole, and it is numerically equal to the atomic mass (for an element) or formula mass (for a compound) read off the periodic table in atomic mass units — the periodic table's listed atomic mass already tells you both numbers at once. For a compound, molar mass is found by multiplying each element's atomic mass by how many atoms of that element appear in the formula (its subscript) and summing the results; a subscript outside a set of parentheses, as in calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂, multiplies every atom inside the parentheses, so that formula contains one calcium, two oxygens, and two hydrogens. Once molar mass is known, it converts freely between mass and moles: moles equal mass in grams divided by molar mass, and mass in grams equals moles multiplied by molar mass. Moles in turn convert to a particle count by multiplying by Avogadro's number, so mass, moles, and number of particles form a chain that can be crossed in either direction as long as molar mass and Avogadro's number are the links.

sections.heading: Worked example: bond type and mass for a magnesium chloride sample

entries.label: Scenario

content.value: A middle-school science teacher is preparing a demonstration solution and needs it to contain 0.150 mole of chloride ion (Cl⁻) once magnesium chloride is dissolved in water. Before weighing anything out, the teacher wants to (1) justify, from first principles, that magnesium and chlorine form an ionic compound rather than a covalent one, (2) confirm the correct chemical formula from the ions' charges, (3) find the compound's molar mass, and (4) use the required amount of chloride ion to calculate exactly how many grams of the solid compound to weigh out.

entries.label: Step 1 — Predict the bond type from electronegativity difference

content.value: Magnesium (Mg) has an electronegativity of about 1.31 on the Pauling scale; chlorine (Cl) has an electronegativity of about 3.16. The difference is 3.16 − 1.31 = 1.85. That difference is well above the roughly 1.7–2.0 cutoff used to predict ionic bonding, and it is reinforced by the identity of the atoms themselves: magnesium is a metal from group 2 with a low ionization energy, so it readily gives up electrons, while chlorine is a reactive nonmetal from group 17 with a high electronegativity, so it readily accepts them. Both the electronegativity gap and the metal-plus-nonmetal pairing point the same direction, so magnesium and chlorine are predicted to bond ionically, transferring electrons rather than sharing them.

entries.label: Step 2 — Determine the correct formula from ionic charges

content.value: Magnesium is in group 2, so a neutral Mg atom has 2 valence electrons; it reaches a stable noble-gas configuration by losing both, forming Mg²⁺. Chlorine is in group 17, so a neutral Cl atom has 7 valence electrons; it reaches a stable configuration by gaining just 1 more, forming Cl⁻. A neutral compound requires the total positive charge to equal the total negative charge. One Mg²⁺ ion contributes +2, and each Cl⁻ ion contributes −1, so two chloride ions are needed to balance one magnesium ion: (+2) + 2 × (−1) = 0. The formula is therefore MgCl₂, with a 1-to-2 ratio of magnesium to chlorine — not a 1-to-1 ratio, which would leave a net +1 charge unbalanced.

entries.label: Step 3 — Calculate the molar mass of MgCl₂

content.value: Molar mass is the sum of each element's atomic mass, multiplied by its subscript in the formula. From the periodic table, magnesium's atomic mass is 24.31 g/mol and chlorine's is 35.45 g/mol. MgCl₂ contains one magnesium atom and two chlorine atoms, so: molar mass = (1 × 24.31 g/mol) + (2 × 35.45 g/mol) = 24.31 g/mol + 70.90 g/mol = 95.21 g/mol. One mole of magnesium chloride has a mass of 95.21 grams.

entries.label: Step 4 — Convert the required moles of chloride ion to moles of compound

content.value: The teacher needs 0.150 mole of Cl⁻ ion, but the quantity to weigh out is measured in moles of the compound MgCl₂, not moles of the ion alone. Because each formula unit of MgCl₂ releases two Cl⁻ ions when it dissolves, moles of Cl⁻ are always twice moles of MgCl₂. Solving for moles of compound: moles of MgCl₂ = (moles of Cl⁻) ÷ 2 = 0.150 mol ÷ 2 = 0.0750 mol. So 0.0750 mole of solid MgCl₂ will supply exactly 0.150 mole of chloride ion once it dissolves.

entries.label: Step 5 — Convert moles of compound to a mass in grams

content.value: With molar mass and the required moles both known, mass = moles × molar mass. Mass = 0.0750 mol × 95.21 g/mol. Multiplying: 0.0750 × 95.21 = 0.0750 × 95 + 0.0750 × 0.21 = 7.125 + 0.01575 = 7.14075 g. Rounded to three significant figures — matching the three significant figures in the given 0.150 mol — the teacher should weigh out 7.14 grams of MgCl₂.

entries.label: Conclusion

content.value: Every stage of the problem feeds the next: the electronegativity difference (1.85) and the metal/nonmetal pairing establish that the bond is ionic, the balance of ionic charges (Mg²⁺ with two Cl⁻) fixes the formula as MgCl₂, the periodic table's atomic masses fix the molar mass at 95.21 g/mol, the 2-to-1 ratio of chloride ions to formula units converts the target of 0.150 mol Cl⁻ into 0.0750 mol MgCl₂, and multiplying by molar mass converts that mole quantity into a weighable mass of 7.14 g. The general pattern worth carrying into any similar item — a target amount of one ion, atom, or fragment inside a compound, translated into a mass of the whole compound to measure out — is to convert to moles of the whole formula unit first, using the subscript as the conversion factor, and only then multiply by molar mass; multiplying the ion's moles directly by the compound's molar mass, skipping that conversion, is the single most common way this kind of problem goes wrong.

entries.label: Mistake: using atomic number instead of atomic mass, or dropping a subscript

content.value: The periodic table lists two different numbers for every element, and confusing them is the single most common arithmetic slip in this category. Atomic number (the small whole number, usually above the element symbol) is the count of protons and identifies the element; it has nothing to do with mass and must never be plugged into a molar-mass calculation. Atomic mass (the decimal number, usually below the symbol) is the quantity that belongs in a molar-mass sum. A closely related error is forgetting that a formula's subscript multiplies every atom of that element, and, for a subscript outside parentheses, every atom inside them — treating Ca(OH)₂ as containing one oxygen and one hydrogen instead of two of each is a frequent miscount, and it silently understates the molar mass by the mass of one O and one H. When a computed molar mass looks suspiciously close to the mass of a single atom rather than a full formula unit, that is usually the tell that a subscript was dropped.

entries.label: Mistake: applying the electronegativity-difference threshold blindly

content.value: The electronegativity-difference cutoffs for ionic, polar covalent, and nonpolar covalent bonding are a useful estimate, not an exact law, and treating the number as the whole answer produces wrong predictions at the edges. Two atoms of the same metal, or two different metals, bond metallically no matter what electronegativity difference a table produces, because metallic bonding is defined by delocalized electrons among metal atoms, not by a numeric gap; the electronegativity-difference rule was built for metal-nonmetal or nonmetal-nonmetal pairs and does not apply when both atoms are metals. A second frequent error is forgetting that the numeric cutoffs are approximate and treating a compound right at the boundary — hydrogen fluoride, for instance, has an electronegativity difference near the ionic/polar-covalent line yet behaves as a polar covalent molecule — as automatically ionic just because the subtracted number looks large; the identity of the atoms (are both nonmetals, so electrons are being shared at all) should always be checked alongside the number, not skipped in favor of it.

entries.label: Mistake: miscounting valence electrons or stopping before every atom has an octet

content.value: A Lewis structure is only as correct as its starting electron count, and the most common failure is getting that count wrong before a single bond is drawn — forgetting to add or subtract electrons for a polyatomic ion's charge is especially frequent, since a 2− ion such as the carbonate ion needs two extra electrons added to the sum of the atoms' group numbers, and a cation needs electrons subtracted. A second common failure is stopping after drawing only single bonds: if placing lone pairs on every outer atom and any leftover electrons on the central atom still leaves the central atom short of eight electrons, one or more outer atoms must convert a lone pair into a second or third shared pair to form a double or triple bond — carbon dioxide's central carbon is not satisfied by two single bonds to oxygen, and needs two double bonds instead. Finally, remember the two standing exceptions before flagging a structure as wrong: hydrogen is complete with two electrons rather than eight, and period-3-or-lower central atoms (such as phosphorus or sulfur) may legitimately exceed an octet, so a structure that looks "over-full" around one of those atoms is not automatically an error.

entries.label: Mistake: reporting the electron-domain geometry as the molecular geometry

content.value: Electron-domain geometry describes how all the electron domains (bonding pairs and lone pairs alike) are arranged around the central atom; molecular geometry describes only where the atoms end up, and the two names diverge as soon as a lone pair is present. The recurring error is reading off the electron-domain arrangement and reporting it as the molecule's shape — calling water "tetrahedral" because it has four electron domains, when the two lone pairs are invisible in the actual atomic arrangement and the molecule is properly described as bent. The fix is to always count domains first to get the electron-domain geometry, and then separately ask how many of those domains are lone pairs before naming the molecular geometry: four domains with zero lone pairs is tetrahedral (methane), with one lone pair is trigonal pyramidal (ammonia), and with two lone pairs is bent (water) — same starting domain count, three different molecular shapes. A second, smaller version of this mistake is forgetting that lone pairs compress the angles between the remaining bonding pairs, so predicting an exact 109.5° bond angle for a molecule that actually has one or more lone pairs on its central atom will be measurably too large.

entries.label: Ohm's law and circuit quantities

content.value: Ohm's law ties together the three quantities that describe a simple electric circuit: voltage V (measured in volts), current I (measured in amperes), and resistance R (measured in ohms), related by V = I × R. Voltage is the electrical potential difference that pushes charge through a circuit — think of it as the "push" supplied by a battery or other source. Current is the rate at which charge flows past a point, and resistance is whatever in the circuit opposes that flow, converting some electrical energy into heat (and, in a bulb, light) along the way. The same relationship can be rearranged to solve for whichever quantity a question asks for: I = V ÷ R when current is unknown, and R = V ÷ I when resistance is unknown. A second useful relationship, electrical power, is P = I × V (watts), which connects a device's power rating back to these same circuit quantities. Before combining resistors into a circuit, make sure each of these individual quantities and its unit is second nature, because the series and parallel rules below build directly on it.

entries.label: Series circuits

content.value: In a series circuit, all of the components are connected end to end along a single path, so there is only one route for charge to take. Because there is nowhere else for the charge to go, the current I is the same at every point in a series circuit — the current through the battery, through the first resistor, and through the last resistor are all identical. Resistances in series simply add: R total = R1 + R2 + R3 + …, and the total is always larger than any individual resistor in the chain, because each additional resistor gives the current one more obstacle to get past. Voltage behaves the opposite way: the source voltage is divided among the components, with each resistor's individual voltage drop given by Ohm's law applied to that resistor alone (V = I × R, using the one shared current), and the drops across every component in the loop add up to the total source voltage. This is also why one burned-out bulb in a series string of lights turns the whole string off: breaking the single path removes the only route the current had.

entries.label: Parallel circuits

content.value: In a parallel circuit, components are connected across the same two points, so each one has its own independent path from the source and its own path back. Because every branch reconnects to the same two points, the voltage across each parallel branch is identical and equal to the source voltage — this is the mirror image of the series rule, where current, not voltage, was the shared quantity. Current, on the other hand, splits among the branches: the current through each branch is set by that branch's own resistance (I = V ÷ R, using the one shared voltage), and the branch currents add up to the total current leaving the source. The equivalent resistance of resistors in parallel follows 1/R total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 + …, and the result is always smaller than the smallest individual branch resistance, because adding a parallel branch gives the charge an additional path and therefore lowers the overall opposition to flow. This is why adding another appliance to a household outlet, which is wired in parallel, does not dim the others — each device sees the full outlet voltage regardless of what else is plugged in.

entries.label: Magnetism and electromagnetic induction

content.value: Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and the region around it where its influence can be detected is its magnetic field, conventionally drawn as field lines that emerge from the north pole, loop around, and re-enter at the south pole; like poles repel and unlike poles attract. A moving electric charge, and therefore an electric current, also creates a magnetic field — a straight current-carrying wire produces a field that circles the wire, and coiling that wire into a loop concentrates and aligns those circling fields to produce a field much like a bar magnet's, called an electromagnet; wrapping the coil around an iron core strengthens the effect further because the iron's own magnetic domains align with the coil's field. The reverse effect, electromagnetic induction, is what makes generators and transformers work: a changing magnetic field passing through a loop of wire induces a voltage — and, in a closed circuit, a current — in that loop. The key word is changing: a stationary magnet sitting inside a stationary coil induces nothing at all, no matter how strong its field is. Only a change in the magnetic flux through the coil, produced by moving the magnet, moving the coil, or varying the current in a nearby coil, induces a current — which is the principle behind a generator, where mechanical motion rotates a coil within a magnetic field to produce a continually changing flux.

entries.label: Wave properties and wave speed

content.value: A wave carries energy from one place to another without carrying matter along with it, and every periodic wave can be described using the same handful of properties. Wavelength (λ) is the distance covered by one complete cycle of the wave — crest to next crest, or trough to next trough — usually measured in meters. Frequency (f) is the number of complete cycles that pass a fixed point per second, measured in hertz (Hz), and amplitude is the maximum displacement of the wave from its undisturbed rest position, which corresponds to how much energy the wave carries rather than to its pitch or color. These quantities are tied together by the wave speed equation, v = f × λ: for a wave moving at a fixed speed, frequency and wavelength are inversely related, so a higher frequency means a proportionally shorter wavelength. Waves also come in two basic types distinguished by how the medium moves relative to the direction the wave travels: in a transverse wave, such as a wave on a string, the medium oscillates perpendicular to the direction of travel, producing crests and troughs, while in a longitudinal wave, such as sound moving through air, the medium oscillates parallel to the direction of travel, producing alternating compressions and rarefactions.

sections.heading: Worked example: a mixed series-parallel circuit

entries.label: Scenario

content.value: A 24 V battery is connected to a circuit built from three resistors. A 2 Ω resistor (R1) is wired directly in series with the battery. After R1, the circuit splits into two branches connected in parallel with each other: a 6 Ω resistor (R2) and a 3 Ω resistor (R3), which reconnect into a single wire that returns to the battery. Find the circuit's total equivalent resistance, the total current supplied by the battery, the voltage drop across R1, and the current through each of R2 and R3.

entries.label: Step 1 — combine the parallel branch

content.value: Before the whole circuit can be treated as one equivalent resistance, the parallel section has to be collapsed into a single value, because R1 is in series with the combination of R2 and R3, not with each of them separately. For resistors in parallel, 1/R parallel = 1/R2 + 1/R3 = 1/6 + 1/3. Writing both fractions over a common denominator of 6 gives 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2, so R parallel = 2 Ω. As a quick sanity check, 2 Ω is smaller than either branch resistor, 6 Ω or 3 Ω, which is exactly what the parallel rule predicts.

entries.label: Step 2 — find the total equivalent resistance

content.value: With the parallel pair replaced by its single 2 Ω equivalent, the circuit is now just R1 in series with that 2 Ω equivalent: R total = R1 + R parallel = 2 Ω + 2 Ω = 4 Ω. That is the resistance the battery effectively "sees" for the whole circuit.

entries.label: Step 3 — find the total current from the battery

content.value: Applying Ohm's law to the whole circuit, using the full 24 V source and the 4 Ω total resistance: I total = V ÷ R total = 24 V ÷ 4 Ω = 6 A. This is the current that leaves the battery and flows through R1, since R1 sits on the single path before the circuit splits into two branches.

entries.label: Step 4 — find the voltage across R1 and across the parallel section

content.value: R1 carries the full 6 A found in Step 3, so its voltage drop is V(R1) = I total × R1 = 6 A × 2 Ω = 12 V. Because the two voltage drops in this series arrangement — R1's drop and the parallel section's drop — must add up to the battery's 24 V, the parallel section's voltage drop is 24 V − 12 V = 12 V. As a check, the same value follows directly from Ohm's law applied to the parallel equivalent: V(parallel) = I total × R parallel = 6 A × 2 Ω = 12 V, which matches.

entries.label: Step 5 — find the current through R2 and through R3

content.value: Both R2 and R3 sit across the same two points, so both see the full 12 V found in Step 4 — the defining feature of a parallel connection. Applying Ohm's law to each branch separately: I(R2) = V ÷ R2 = 12 V ÷ 6 Ω = 2 A, and I(R3) = V ÷ R3 = 12 V ÷ 3 Ω = 4 A. As a check, the two branch currents should add back up to the 6 A total current found in Step 3: 2 A + 4 A = 6 A, which confirms the arithmetic.

entries.label: Answer

content.value: Total equivalent resistance: 4 Ω. Total current from the battery: 6 A. Voltage drop across R1: 12 V. Current through R2: 2 A. Current through R3: 4 A. Every intermediate result was checked against an independent relationship — the parallel resistance against "smaller than either branch," the voltage split against the battery's total, and the branch currents against the total current — which is a habit worth carrying into any multi-step circuit problem: each step gives a second way to catch an arithmetic slip before it reaches the final answer.

entries.label: Mistake: swapping the series and parallel resistance formulas

content.value: The single most common circuit-analysis error is swapping the two combination formulas: adding resistors that are actually in parallel, or taking reciprocals of resistors that are actually in series. Resistances in series simply add (R total = R1 + R2 + …) and the result is always larger than any individual resistor. Resistances in parallel combine by reciprocals (1/R total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …) and the result is always smaller than the smallest individual resistor. That second fact is the fastest way to catch the error: if a "parallel" answer choice is larger than either original resistor, it cannot be right, no matter how the arithmetic was done. For exactly two resistors in parallel, the shortcut R total = (R1 × R2) ÷ (R1 + R2) — "product over sum" — gives the same answer as the reciprocal method without an extra fraction step, but it only works for two resistors at a time.

entries.label: Mistake: mixing up which quantity stays constant

content.value: Test-takers frequently mix up which quantity stays the same and which one splits, because the two circuit types are mirror images of each other. In series, current is the same everywhere along the single path, and voltage is what divides among the components. In parallel, voltage is the same across every branch, since each branch connects the same two points, and current is what divides among the branches. A fast way to keep them straight: series has one path, so there is only one current to share among all the components as voltage drops; parallel has multiple paths, so there is only one voltage that every branch independently sees, and the available current divides according to each branch's own resistance.

entries.label: Mistake: mishandling frequency and wavelength in v = f × λ

content.value: Because the wave speed equation v = f × λ links frequency and wavelength together, it is easy to plug values into the wrong place — most often, multiplying when the problem calls for division, or dividing speed by frequency when speed and wavelength are known and frequency is what's missing. The fix is to keep the relationship's shape firmly in mind: at a fixed wave speed, frequency and wavelength move in opposite directions, so doubling one must halve the other. A quick unit check also catches most slips: frequency in hertz (cycles per second) times wavelength in meters gives meters per second, which is a speed — if an answer's units do not come out that way, the wrong operation was used. It is worth remembering that visible light, sound, and every other wave family obey exactly this same relationship, even though the numeric values involved, such as the speed of light versus the speed of sound, differ enormously.

entries.label: Mistake: mistaking a static field for a changing one, and confusing wave-particle motion

content.value: Two related misconceptions are worth naming together, because both involve mistaking a static condition for a dynamic one. First, electromagnetic induction requires a changing magnetic flux, not merely the presence of a magnetic field — a stationary magnet resting inside a stationary coil induces no current at all, however strong the magnet is, and a common wrong answer on this topic assumes any nearby magnetic field automatically produces current. Second, candidates often confuse how the medium itself moves in a transverse wave versus a longitudinal wave: in a transverse wave, individual particles of the medium move perpendicular to the direction the wave travels, while in a longitudinal wave, the particles move back and forth parallel to the direction of travel, compressing and expanding the medium rather than rising and falling. In neither wave type does the medium itself travel from source to observer — only the disturbance, and the energy it carries, propagates outward while each particle oscillates about a fixed average position.

entries.label: Forms of energy and conservation of energy

content.value: Energy shows up in a handful of recognizable forms — kinetic (motion), gravitational potential (position in a field), elastic potential (a stretched or compressed spring), chemical potential (stored in bonds, released or absorbed as bonds break and form), thermal (the disordered kinetic energy of a substance's particles), electrical, and radiant (light and other electromagnetic waves). The law of conservation of energy says the total energy of an isolated system never changes; energy only converts from one form to another or transfers from one object to another, and none is created or destroyed. A dropped ball converts gravitational potential energy to kinetic energy on the way down and, on impact, to thermal energy and sound; a battery converts stored chemical energy to electrical energy, and a bulb converts most of that electrical energy to light and the rest to unwanted thermal energy. "Energy loss" in a real system almost always means a conversion to thermal energy that spreads into the surroundings rather than a violation of the conservation law — friction, air resistance, and electrical resistance are the usual culprits. For test purposes, treat any system described as closed or isolated as one where you can set total energy before equal to total energy after, even as the mix of forms changes.

entries.label: Temperature versus heat versus thermal energy

content.value: These three words get used interchangeably in casual speech, and untangling them is one of the most heavily tested ideas in this category. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a sample — it does not depend on how much of the substance you have. Thermal energy (sometimes called internal energy) is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles in a sample, and it does depend on amount: a swimming pool at 25 degrees Celsius has far more thermal energy than a teaspoon of water at the same 25 degrees Celsius, even though their temperatures — and therefore their average particle kinetic energy — are identical. Heat is neither of those; heat is energy in transit, specifically the energy that flows from a higher-temperature object to a lower-temperature object because of that temperature difference. Once the transfer stops, it is no longer meaningful to call the energy in either object "heat" — an object does not "contain" heat, it contains thermal energy, and it "gives off" or "absorbs" heat only while a temperature difference is actively driving a transfer. Keeping these three nouns — temperature, thermal energy, heat — mapped to average, total, and in-transit will resolve most tricky wording on this topic.

entries.label: Specific heat capacity and q = m × c × ΔT

content.value: Specific heat capacity (c) is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of one gram (or one kilogram, depending on the unit system) of a substance by one degree Celsius. It is a property of the material, not of any particular sample of it — water's specific heat is about 4.18 joules per gram per degree Celsius regardless of whether you have one gram or one kilogram of it, and metals typically have much smaller specific heats than water (aluminum is about 0.90 J/(g·°C), roughly a fifth of water's). A high specific heat means the substance resists temperature change: it takes a large amount of energy to heat it up a little, and it releases a large amount of energy while cooling down a little, which is exactly why coastal climates are milder than inland climates at the same latitude — large bodies of water buffer temperature swings. The relationship connecting heat, mass, specific heat, and temperature change is q = m × c × ΔT, where q is the heat transferred (joules), m is the mass, c is the specific heat, and ΔT is the temperature change (final minus initial). This equation only applies within a single phase — it describes warming or cooling liquid water, for instance, but not the process of turning liquid water into steam at a constant 100 degrees Celsius.

entries.label: Phase changes and latent heat

content.value: When a substance is at the temperature where it changes phase (its melting point or boiling point), added or removed heat does not change its temperature — a thermometer in a beaker of ice and water sitting at 0 degrees Celsius will read 0 degrees Celsius continuously while the ice melts, even as a burner keeps adding energy underneath. That energy is going into breaking (melting, boiling) or forming (freezing, condensing) the intermolecular bonds that hold the substance in its more-ordered phase, rather than into speeding up particle motion, so the temperature plateaus on a heating or cooling curve during the entire phase change and only resumes rising or falling once the phase change is complete. The energy required is called latent heat, and it is calculated with a different equation than sensible heating: q = m × L, where L is the latent heat of fusion (for melting/freezing) or latent heat of vaporization (for boiling/condensing), and there is no ΔT term because temperature is not changing. Latent heat of vaporization is typically much larger than latent heat of fusion for the same substance — water's is about 2260 J/g for vaporization versus about 334 J/g for fusion — which is why steam at 100 degrees Celsius carries far more energy, and causes far worse burns, than the same mass of boiling-hot liquid water at the same temperature.

entries.label: Thermal equilibrium and the three heat-transfer mechanisms

content.value: Two objects placed in contact exchange heat until they reach thermal equilibrium — the point at which both are at the same temperature and net heat flow between them stops (individual particles still exchange energy at the boundary, but the flow in each direction balances out). Heat always flows spontaneously from higher to lower temperature, never the reverse, without external work being done on the system. Heat moves by three distinct mechanisms, and exam items often hinge on picking the right one for a described situation. Conduction is transfer through direct particle-to-particle contact, most efficient in solids where particles are packed closely and vibrate against their neighbors — a metal spoon heating up in a hot pot. Convection is transfer through the bulk movement of a fluid (liquid or gas): a heated fluid becomes less dense, rises, and is replaced by cooler, denser fluid, setting up a circulating current — this is how a pot of soup heats throughout, and how a radiator warms a room. Radiation is transfer by electromagnetic waves and is the only mechanism that requires no medium at all, which is how the sun's energy crosses the vacuum of space to reach Earth. Most real situations involve more than one mechanism at once — a campfire warms nearby skin mainly by radiation while also heating the surrounding air by convection.

sections.heading: Worked example: finding the equilibrium temperature of a metal-water mixture

entries.label: Scenario

content.value: A 200 g block of aluminum is heated to 100.0 degrees Celsius and then dropped into 300 g of water sitting at 20.0 degrees Celsius inside an insulated (perfectly heat-isolated) container. The specific heat of aluminum is 0.90 J/(g·°C) and the specific heat of water is 4.18 J/(g·°C). Assuming no heat escapes to the container or the surrounding air, find the final equilibrium temperature of the aluminum-water system.

entries.label: Step 1 — Set up the governing relationship

content.value: Because the container is insulated, the only place heat can go is from the hotter object (the aluminum, starting at 100.0 °C) into the cooler object (the water, starting at 20.0 °C). Energy conservation means the heat lost by the aluminum as it cools must exactly equal the heat gained by the water as it warms: heat lost by aluminum = heat gained by water. Writing q = m × c × ΔT for each side, with T_f standing for the shared final temperature both substances reach: m_Al × c_Al × (T_initial,Al − T_f) = m_water × c_water × (T_f − T_initial,water). Each ΔT is written so it comes out positive — the aluminum's drop in temperature on the left, the water's rise in temperature on the right — which keeps both sides representing a positive quantity of heat.

entries.label: Step 2 — Substitute the known values

content.value: Plugging in the numbers: 200 g × 0.90 J/(g·°C) × (100.0 °C − T_f) = 300 g × 4.18 J/(g·°C) × (T_f − 20.0 °C). First, multiply mass by specific heat on each side to simplify the coefficients: 200 × 0.90 = 180 J/°C on the left, and 300 × 4.18 = 1254 J/°C on the right. The equation is now: 180 × (100.0 − T_f) = 1254 × (T_f − 20.0), where 180 and 1254 are each object's total heat capacity in joules per degree Celsius — the amount of heat that object exchanges per degree it changes.

entries.label: Step 3 — Distribute and solve for T_f

content.value: Distribute both sides: 180 × 100.0 − 180 × T_f = 1254 × T_f − 1254 × 20.0, which gives 18,000 − 180 T_f = 1254 T_f − 25,080. Collect the T_f terms on one side and the constants on the other by adding 180 T_f and 25,080 to both sides: 18,000 + 25,080 = 1254 T_f + 180 T_f, which is 43,080 = 1434 T_f. Divide both sides by 1434: T_f = 43,080 ÷ 1434 = 30.04 °C. Rounded to three significant figures, the equilibrium temperature is 30.0 °C.

entries.label: Step 4 — Sanity-check the answer

content.value: Two quick checks confirm this is reasonable before moving on. First, T_f must land between the two starting temperatures (20.0 °C and 100.0 °C) — 30.0 °C does. Second, because the water's total heat capacity (1254 J/°C) is roughly seven times larger than the aluminum's (180 J/°C), the water should dominate the outcome and pull the final temperature much closer to its own starting point of 20.0 °C than to the aluminum's 100.0 °C — and 30.0 °C, only 10 degrees above water's start but 70 degrees below aluminum's start, matches that expectation. As a final numeric check, plug T_f = 30.04 °C back into each side separately: the aluminum loses 180 × (100.0 − 30.04) = 180 × 69.96 ≈ 12,593 J, and the water gains 1254 × (30.04 − 20.0) = 1254 × 10.04 ≈ 12,590 J — equal within rounding, confirming the heat lost by the aluminum matches the heat gained by the water.

entries.label: Answer

content.value: The aluminum-water system reaches thermal equilibrium at approximately 30.0 degrees Celsius.

entries.label: Mistake: treating temperature as if it were the amount of thermal energy

content.value: A very common trap is assuming that two samples at the same temperature must hold the same amount of energy, or that the sample with the higher temperature always holds more total energy. Temperature depends only on average particle kinetic energy, not on how much substance is present, so a large sample at a modest temperature can easily hold more total thermal energy than a small sample at a much higher temperature — a bathtub of lukewarm water has far more thermal energy than a lit match, even though the match is hotter. Whenever a question describes two objects of different mass or asks which one "has more energy," check whether it is asking about temperature (average) or thermal energy (total, which depends on mass and specific heat too) before answering.

entries.label: Mistake: applying q = mcΔT straight through a phase change

content.value: When a problem asks for the total heat needed to take a substance from, say, solid below its melting point to liquid above its melting point, it is tempting to use one q = mcΔT calculation across the whole temperature span. That skips the plateau: the heat needed to actually melt the substance (q = mL, using the latent heat of fusion) at the constant melting-point temperature does not appear anywhere in a single mcΔT calculation, and specific heat is different in each phase besides. The correct approach treats a multi-stage heating (or cooling) process as separate legs — heat the solid to its melting point with q = mcΔT using the solid's specific heat, melt it at constant temperature with q = mL, then heat the resulting liquid to the target temperature with q = mcΔT using the liquid's specific heat — and adds the three (or more) quantities of heat together. Forgetting a leg, or forgetting that temperature does not move during the melting or boiling leg, is the single most common error in multi-step heating-curve problems.

entries.label: Mistake: sign and setup errors in heat-exchange (mixing) problems

content.value: In a two-substance mixing problem, the heat lost by the hotter object and the heat gained by the cooler object must come out equal in magnitude — losing track of which ΔT should be positive is what causes wrong answers here. A safe way to avoid sign trouble is to always write each ΔT as (higher value − lower value) so both sides of the heat-lost-equals-heat-gained equation come out positive, exactly as in the worked example above, rather than trying to carry negative signs through m × c × (T_final − T_initial) for the cooling object. After solving, always confirm the resulting equilibrium temperature falls between the two starting temperatures — an answer outside that range is a guaranteed sign or algebra error, not a valid physical outcome.

entries.label: Mistake: unit mismatches and forgetting the insulated-system assumption

content.value: Two smaller but frequent slips round out this list. First, unit consistency: mass must be in the same unit the specific heat's value is defined for (grams with J/(g·°C), or kilograms with J/(kg·°C)) and mixing grams into a kilogram-based specific heat — or vice versa — throws the answer off by a factor of 1000. Note also that because ΔT is a difference, converting both temperatures to Kelvin before subtracting is unnecessary busywork that changes nothing: a one-degree change is the same size in Celsius and in Kelvin, so ΔT in Celsius and ΔT in Kelvin are numerically identical. Second, calorimetry problems on this exam almost always specify (or imply) an idealized, perfectly insulated system so that q_lost = q_gained holds exactly; real calorimeters lose some heat to the container and surrounding air, which is why real experimental measurements of specific heat tend to run slightly off from published reference values. Recognize the phrase "insulated container" or "no heat lost to the surroundings" as the signal that the simple equal-and-opposite heat equation applies without any additional correction term.

sections.heading: Concept overview: kinematics, Newton's laws, energy, momentum, and circular motion

entries.label: Position, velocity, acceleration, and the kinematics toolkit

content.value: Position, velocity, and acceleration describe motion in increasing order of change: velocity is the rate of change of position (how fast and in what direction something moves), and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity (how fast and in what direction the velocity itself is changing). All three are vectors in general, but on this exam most kinematics problems are one-dimensional, so a sign (+ or -) stands in for direction: pick a positive direction once at the start of a problem and stay consistent, because a negative velocity means motion in the chosen negative direction, not slowing down, and a negative acceleration means the velocity is changing in the negative direction, which speeds an object up if it is already moving in that direction rather than always slowing it down. For motion with constant acceleration, four equations tie position, velocity, acceleration, and time together: v = v0 + at; d = v0t + (1/2)at^2; v^2 = v0^2 + 2ad; and d = ((v0 + v)/2)t, the last of which uses the fact that average velocity under constant acceleration is just the average of the initial and final velocities. Free fall is the single most common special case: near Earth's surface, ignoring air resistance, every object accelerates downward at g ≈ 9.8 m/s^2 regardless of its mass, so the same four equations apply with a = -g (or +g, depending on which direction was chosen as positive) plugged in directly.

entries.label: Newton's three laws and force diagrams

content.value: Newton's first law (inertia) says an object's velocity does not change unless a net external force acts on it: an object at rest stays at rest, and an object moving at constant velocity keeps moving at that same speed and direction on its own, with zero net force required. Newton's second law quantifies what happens when the net force is not zero: net force equals mass times acceleration, Fnet = ma, so acceleration points in the same direction as the net force and is proportional to it and inversely proportional to mass. Newton's third law says forces come in pairs: whenever object A exerts a force on object B, object B exerts an equal and opposite force back on object A, and because these two forces act on two different objects, they never cancel each other out for either object individually. A force diagram (free-body diagram) isolates one object and draws every external force acting on it — weight (mg, always straight down), the normal force (perpendicular to the contact surface, pushing the object away from it), applied forces, tension, and friction (opposing relative sliding, parallel to the surface) — as arrows sized roughly by magnitude. Once every force is drawn, the net force in each direction is the vector sum of the forces in that direction, and Fnet = ma is applied separately along each independent axis, most commonly horizontal and vertical.

entries.label: Work and energy

content.value: Work is done on an object when a force acts on it through a displacement, and for a constant force it equals W = Fd cos(theta), where theta is the angle between the force and the displacement — a force perpendicular to the motion, such as the normal force on a horizontally sliding object, does zero work no matter how large it is. Kinetic energy is the energy of motion, KE = (1/2)mv^2, and gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface is PE = mgh, measured relative to some chosen reference height. The work-energy theorem connects the two: the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy, Wnet = deltaKE = KEfinal - KEinitial, which lets a final speed be found from forces and distance without working through the kinematics equations, or the reverse. In a system with no friction or other non-conservative forces, total mechanical energy (KE + PE) is conserved — energy converts between kinetic and potential but the sum stays constant, which is the basis for problems like an object sliding down a frictionless ramp or swinging on a pendulum. When friction or another non-conservative force is present, mechanical energy is not conserved; the work done against friction is the amount by which KE + PE decreases, and that lost mechanical energy is converted to heat.

entries.label: Momentum and collisions

content.value: Momentum is p = mv, a vector that points in the same direction as velocity, and for an isolated system (no net external force) total momentum is conserved — the vector sum of every object's momentum before an interaction equals the vector sum after, even though individual objects' momenta can change enormously. This is the tool of choice for collisions and explosions, where the forces objects exert on each other during the brief contact are internal to the system and equal and opposite by Newton's third law, so they cancel in the total. Collisions are classified by what happens to kinetic energy. In a perfectly elastic collision, both momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved — objects bounce off each other, and if both masses and one set of velocities are known, momentum conservation gives one equation and kinetic energy conservation gives a second, enough to solve for two unknown final velocities. In a perfectly inelastic collision, the objects stick together and move with one common final velocity afterward; momentum is still conserved, but kinetic energy is not — some is converted to heat, sound, and deformation. Most real collisions fall somewhere in between: momentum conservation always applies to an isolated system, but kinetic energy conservation is a special property only elastic collisions have, so it should never be assumed unless a problem states the collision is elastic.

entries.label: Circular motion and centripetal force

content.value: An object moving at constant speed around a circular path is still accelerating, because its velocity's direction is continuously changing even though its magnitude (speed) is not. That acceleration, called centripetal acceleration, always points from the object toward the center of the circle, perpendicular to the velocity at every instant, and has magnitude ac = v^2/r, where r is the radius of the circular path. By Newton's second law, sustaining this acceleration requires a net force pointed toward the center as well — the centripetal force, Fc = mac = mv^2/r. Centripetal force is not a new, separate kind of force the way gravity or friction are; it is simply the name given to whichever combination of the real forces already acting — tension in a string, gravity, friction between tires and road, the normal force from a curved track — happens to supply the center-directed net force in a given situation. A common exam setup is a car rounding a flat curve, where friction between the tires and the road supplies the centripetal force, or a ball on a string swung in a horizontal circle, where the horizontal component of the string's tension supplies it. If the required centripetal force exceeds what the available force can provide — friction, for instance, has a maximum value before the tires slip — the object cannot maintain the circular path and moves in a straighter line instead.

sections.heading: Worked example: pushing a box across a rough floor

entries.label: Scenario

content.value: A 12 kg box, initially at rest on a horizontal floor, is pushed with a constant horizontal applied force of 50 N. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the box and the floor is 0.25. Using g = 9.8 m/s^2, find (a) the box's acceleration while the force is applied, (b) its speed after 4.0 seconds, and (c) how far it travels in that time.

entries.label: Step 1 — draw the free-body diagram and identify the forces

content.value: Four forces act on the box: its weight (mg, straight down), the normal force from the floor (N, straight up), the applied push (Fapplied = 50 N, horizontal, in the direction of motion), and kinetic friction (f, horizontal, opposing the box's motion since it is sliding once it starts to move — friction acts backward, opposite the applied force). Because the box moves horizontally and does not accelerate vertically, the vertical forces must balance even though the horizontal forces do not: N = mg. This vertical balance is what gives the normal force, which in turn is what the friction force depends on.

entries.label: Step 2 — find the normal force and the friction force

content.value: N = mg = 12 kg × 9.8 m/s^2 = 117.6 N. Kinetic friction opposing the motion is f = μk N = 0.25 × 117.6 N = 29.4 N.

entries.label: Step 3 — apply Newton's second law to find the acceleration

content.value: Along the horizontal direction, the net force is the applied push minus the opposing friction force: Fnet = Fapplied - f = 50 N - 29.4 N = 20.6 N, directed in the direction of the push. By Newton's second law, a = Fnet / m = 20.6 N / 12 kg = 1.71667 m/s^2, which rounds to about 1.7 m/s^2. The unrounded value, 1.71667 m/s^2, is carried into the next two steps so rounding error does not creep into the later answers.

entries.label: Step 4 — use kinematics to find the velocity after 4.0 seconds

content.value: The box starts from rest (v0 = 0) and accelerates at a constant 1.71667 m/s^2 for t = 4.0 s. Using v = v0 + at: v = 0 + (1.71667 m/s^2)(4.0 s) = 6.86667 m/s, which rounds to about 6.9 m/s.

entries.label: Step 5 — use kinematics to find the distance traveled

content.value: Using d = v0t + (1/2)at^2 with v0 = 0: d = (1/2)(1.71667 m/s^2)(4.0 s)^2 = (1/2)(1.71667 m/s^2)(16 s^2) = 13.7333 m, which rounds to about 13.7 m. As a check, the same distance follows from the average-velocity form d = ((v0 + v)/2)t = ((0 + 6.86667 m/s)/2)(4.0 s) = (3.43333 m/s)(4.0 s) = 13.7333 m — an exact match, confirming the arithmetic in Steps 3 through 5 is consistent.

entries.label: Conclusion

content.value: The box accelerates at about 1.7 m/s^2, reaches a speed of about 6.9 m/s after 4.0 seconds, and travels about 13.7 m in that time. The two ideas that make the problem tractable are the same two ideas the whole Mechanics category tests: first find the net force from a correct free-body diagram and Newton's second law, then hand the resulting constant acceleration to the kinematics equations to answer questions about speed and distance.

entries.label: Assuming a force is needed to keep something moving

content.value: A deeply intuitive but wrong idea is that a moving object needs a continuing force to keep moving, and that it will naturally slow down and stop once the force is removed. Newton's first law says the opposite: an object moving at constant velocity in a straight line stays that way with zero net force acting on it. Objects in everyday life do seem to slow down when nothing is visibly pushing them, but that is because of an unbalanced force test-takers often forget to draw — friction or air resistance — not because motion itself requires upkeep. When a problem states that an object moves at constant velocity, including constant speed in a straight line, the correct first move is to conclude the net force on it is zero, and then use that fact to solve for an unknown force, such as the exact friction force needed to balance an applied push. Do not confuse "constant velocity" with "no forces act" — multiple forces can act on an object and still sum to zero.

entries.label: Confusing mass with weight

content.value: Mass and weight are often used interchangeably in casual speech, but they are different physical quantities, and this exam expects the distinction. Mass (measured in kilograms) is the amount of matter in an object and a measure of its resistance to acceleration, or inertia; it does not depend on location. Weight (measured in newtons) is the force of gravity on that mass, w = mg, and it does depend on location, since g varies from planet to planet and even slightly across Earth's surface. An object's mass is the same on the Moon as on Earth, but its weight on the Moon is only about one-sixth of its weight on Earth because the Moon's g is about one-sixth of Earth's. A related error is plugging a weight into the wrong side of F = ma without converting: mass belongs in Newton's second law, and if a problem gives weight instead of mass, divide by g first (m = w/g) before using F = ma. Also watch for a problem that gives weight directly where a normal force is needed — in that case N often equals w already, and multiplying by g a second time is a common and easy-to-miss error.

entries.label: Sign and direction errors in one-dimensional kinematics

content.value: Because one-dimensional kinematics represents direction with a plus or minus sign rather than an arrow, sign errors are one of the most common sources of wrong answers even when the underlying physics is understood correctly. The fix is procedural: choose a positive direction before writing down a single number, and apply it consistently to every quantity in the problem — position, velocity, and acceleration alike. A classic trap is an object thrown straight up: if up is chosen positive, velocity starts positive and decreases, because the acceleration due to gravity is negative (-9.8 m/s^2) the entire time, both on the way up and on the way down; velocity reaches zero at the top and becomes negative on the way down, while the acceleration itself never changes sign or magnitude. A second trap is displacement versus distance traveled: if a hiker walks 40 m east and then 30 m west, the total distance traveled is 70 m, but the displacement (final position minus initial position) is only 10 m east, and a question asking for one is not asking for the other. Always reread the question to see whether it wants a signed vector quantity (displacement, velocity, acceleration) or an unsigned scalar (distance, speed).

entries.label: Treating momentum conservation and kinetic-energy conservation as interchangeable

content.value: Momentum is conserved in every collision within an isolated system, elastic or not, but kinetic energy is only conserved in a perfectly elastic collision, and treating the two as interchangeable is one of the most common errors in this category. In a perfectly inelastic collision, where two objects stick together, momentum conservation still gives the correct combined final velocity, but plugging that same scenario into a kinetic-energy-conservation equation gives a wrong answer, because kinetic energy is lost to heat, sound, and deformation during the collision. A second common error is treating momentum as a scalar and simply adding masses times speeds without regard to direction; momentum is a vector, so two objects moving toward each other must have their momenta assigned opposite signs, or opposite-signed components, before being added, and a head-on collision between equal masses moving at equal and opposite speeds sums to zero total momentum, not double the momentum of one object. Finally, remember that Newton's third law is why momentum is conserved in a collision even though large forces act during it: the force each object exerts on the other is equal, opposite, and internal to the two-object system, so it cancels out of the total-momentum bookkeeping regardless of how complicated the collision itself is.

entries.label: The scientific method as a cycle, not a checklist

content.value: Textbooks often draw the scientific method as a straight line — observe, question, hypothesize, experiment, conclude — but working scientists move through it as a loop, and often jump steps or double back. A puzzling observation prompts a question; a hypothesis proposes a testable, tentative explanation; a controlled experiment or a systematic set of observations puts that hypothesis at risk of being wrong; the results either hold up or force a revision of the hypothesis, the question, or even the original observation. What makes an investigation scientific is not that it followed a fixed sequence of numbered steps, but that at every stage a claim was left open to being overturned by evidence. A result that contradicts the hypothesis is not a failed experiment — it is exactly how the method is supposed to work, and it usually generates the next round of questions rather than ending the inquiry. Expect Praxis items to describe an investigation out of textbook order, skip a step, or loop back to revise a hypothesis after unexpected data, and to reward recognizing that this is still good science rather than a broken procedure.

entries.label: Hypothesis, theory, and law are different kinds of claim, not different confidence levels

content.value: These three words name different jobs a scientific claim can do, not three rungs on a ladder of certainty. A hypothesis is a specific, testable, tentative explanation for a particular observation — narrow in scope and often discarded or revised after one round of testing. A scientific theory is a broad, well-substantiated explanatory framework that accounts for a large body of observations, makes predictions, and has survived repeated, varied attempts to disprove it; cell theory, atomic theory, and the theory of plate tectonics are examples. A scientific law is typically a concise statement, often mathematical, that describes a consistent pattern in how something behaves under given conditions — Boyle's law relating pressure and volume, or Newton's law of universal gravitation — without necessarily explaining why the pattern holds. Laws describe what happens; theories explain why. A theory does not graduate into a law after accumulating enough supporting evidence, because the two are not stops on the same track: a law can be as well established as any theory in science and still just describe a pattern, while a theory can be extremely well supported and still be an explanation rather than a description. Both hypotheses and theories can be revised or replaced by better evidence; a law can too, though laws that hold across an enormous range of conditions are revised less often.

entries.label: Variables, controls, and replication in experimental design

content.value: A controlled experiment isolates the effect of one factor by deliberately changing only that factor and holding everything else steady. The independent variable is the one the experimenter deliberately changes across trials; the dependent variable is the one measured, because its value depends on what the independent variable did.
